name: Decaf tea
caffeine: Reduced, not removed: decaf tea keeps a trace of caffeine, so a guest avoiding it on medical advice is better served a tisane.

house.ask: Not printed on the menus: ask at lineup whether the bar pours a decaffeinated tea, which brand and which base tea, and the price.

what: Decaf tea is real tea, Camellia sinensis, with most of its caffeine taken out by carbon dioxide under high pressure, by a solvent such as ethyl acetate or methylene chloride, or by water passed through carbon. It is reduced, not emptied, and a trace remains. It brews like the tea it was made from, black or green, and for a guest who wants no caffeine at all a tisane is the better answer.
taste: Like its base tea, a little thinner and flatter. Carbon dioxide is generally credited with keeping the most flavour, while ethyl acetate is sometimes said to leave a chemical note.

steps: Read the box and brew decaf the way its base tea brews, black or green.
Bring fresh water to a full boil for a black, or let it fall to 160 to 180F (71 to 82C) for a green.
Warm the pot and put in one bag per cup, or 2 to 3 g per 6 to 8 oz.
Pour the water on and steep 3 to 5 minutes for black, 1 to 2 for green, then pull the bag.
Send milk, lemon and sugar on the side as the base tea calls for.
make.ratio: 2 to 3 g of leaf per 6 to 8 oz of water
make.dose: One bag, about 2 g, or 2 to 3 g loose leaf
make.temp: Black 200 to 212F (93 to 100C); green 160 to 180F (71 to 82C)
make.time: 3 to 5 minutes black; 1 to 2 minutes green
make.cup: Warmed pot into a cup or mug, 6 to 8 oz

serve: Serve it as the base tea: a warmed pot or cup, a dish for the bag, and milk, lemon and sugar on the side for a black. Say decaf aloud at the pass and mark the saucer, because it looks exactly like the regular pot. For a guest who wants none at all, offer a tisane before the decaf.
story: Tea is decaffeinated in four main ways: carbon dioxide under high pressure, which pulls the small caffeine molecule and leaves larger flavour molecules; ethyl acetate, sometimes sold as natural because of its natural origin; methylene chloride; and water run through a carbon filter, used for only a few teas. None reaches zero. And a thirty second rinse at the table does nothing useful: it does not decaffeinate a leaf.
guest: Decaf tea still carries a trace of caffeine; if you would rather avoid it altogether, a herbal infusion such as peppermint or rooibos comes from another plant entirely.
watch: Decaffeinated is not caffeine free: say trace, not none, and offer a tisane to a guest avoiding caffeine on medical advice.
A thirty second rinse does not decaffeinate a leaf; never offer it as a fix.
Decaf and regular pots look alike: mark the decaf at the pass so it reaches the right seat.
Not every tisane is caffeine free: yerba mate, guayusa and cascara carry caffeine of their own.

study: Caffeine, and the questions guests ask

recall.prompt: How is decaf tea made, and how do you brew it?
recall.answer: Most caffeine is removed by carbon dioxide, ethyl acetate, methylene chloride or water and carbon, leaving a trace. Brew it as its base tea: a decaf black at a full boil, one bag per cup, 3 to 5 minutes, milk on the side.

quiz.q: Which decaffeination method works with a gas under high pressure?
quiz.explain: Under high pressure, carbon dioxide acts as a solvent that pulls the small caffeine molecule and leaves larger flavour molecules, which is why it is credited with keeping flavour.

quiz.q: A guest avoiding caffeine on medical advice asks for decaf tea. What do you tell them?
options: A long steep removes the rest
Green decaf has none; black has some
It keeps a trace; offer a tisane
quiz.explain: Decaffeinated tea is reduced, not emptied. Say trace, not none, and offer a tisane such as peppermint or rooibos, which is not the tea plant.

quiz.q: Does a thirty second rinse in hot water decaffeinate tea leaf?
options: Yes, most caffeine leaves at once
quiz.explain: A quick rinse does not decaffeinate a leaf. Decaf is made at the factory by carbon dioxide, a solvent or water and carbon, and even that leaves a trace.
